abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Decisions come from gathering noisy evidence until a limit is reached.
This mechanism explains how stimulus strength affects speed, accuracy, and confidence.
More noise should lead to faster choices, lower accuracy, and higher confidence.
Researchers used a new sensory method to mimic brain noise and verified it with monkey recordings.
In humans and monkeys, more noise led to faster and more confident decisions with little accuracy loss.
The results matched the mathematical model's predictions.

sentences.text: Scientists believe that many of the decisions we make every day are the result of the brain gathering evidence until it reaches a specific threshold.
This process involves collecting information that is often imperfect or 'noisy' until enough has been stored to trigger a final choice.
Specifically, the clarity of what we see or hear determines how quickly we decide, how often we are right, and how sure we feel about our choice.
When we look at how we perceive the world, this specific mechanism helps explain how the strength of a signal compared to background noise influences our behavior.
It suggests that if the amount of noise in the information increases, a person should actually make their decision faster.
The theory also leads to a very surprising and counterintuitive prediction regarding the nature of noise itself.
While this extra noise would likely reduce the accuracy of the choice, it is also predicted to paradoxically make the person feel more confident in their answer.
They confirmed that this technique worked as intended by recording the electrical activity of neurons in the visual cortex of macaque monkeys.
To see if these strange predictions were true, the researchers developed a new way to manipulate sensory information that mimics adding random noise directly to the brain's motion-processing centers.
The researchers then tested both human volunteers and monkeys using these noisy visual displays to see how their decision-making changed.
They found that for both species, increasing the noise caused the subjects to make faster decisions and report higher levels of confidence.
This increase in speed and certainty occurred even when the noise was kept at a level that only slightly decreased their overall accuracy.
The actual size of these changes in speed and confidence was remarkably consistent with what the mathematical models of evidence accumulation had predicted.
Ultimately, the study shows that our sense of confidence and our reaction times are deeply tied to how the brain tallies up noisy information until a boundary is hit.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Shigella bacteria use an enzyme called OspI to change a specific building block in the human protein UBC13 from glutamine to glutamate.
This chemical change stops UBC13 from working with another protein called TRAF6, which shuts down the body's inflammatory immune response.
The study shows that this modification prevents UBC13 and TRAF6 from sticking together by disrupting both their stable and temporary connections.
The modification creates a new internal bond within UBC13 that acts like a distraction, stealing away a connection point needed to bind with TRAF6.
This internal competition blocks the short-lived, temporary interactions that are essential for the two proteins to find each other and lock into place.
Additionally, the new chemical group on UBC13 has a negative charge that physically pushes away the negatively charged surface of the TRAF6 protein.
These results reveal how a small chemical modification can destabilize the shape and stability of protein pairs to prevent them from working together.

sentences.text: Shigella flexneri is a type of bacteria that causes severe intestinal illness by releasing a specific enzyme called OspI into human cells.
This bacterial enzyme targets a human protein named UBC13 and performs a chemical reaction that changes one of its amino acid building blocks from glutamine into glutamate.
As a result, the cell's internal alarm system, known as the NF-κB inflammatory response, is effectively silenced, allowing the bacteria to avoid detection by the immune system.
Because of this single chemical change, UBC13 can no longer perform its normal job of tagging other proteins in partnership with a helper protein called TRAF6.
Researchers discovered that this chemical modification, known as deamidation, stops UBC13 and TRAF6 from physically connecting with one another.
The modification works by interfering with both the permanent docking points and the fleeting, temporary contacts that these two proteins usually make when they meet.
Specifically, the change to glutamate creates a new internal attraction within the UBC13 protein itself, forming what scientists call a salt-bridge.
This new internal bond is a problem because it uses up a part of the protein that is normally required to form a critical bridge between UBC13 and TRAF6.
By competing for this connection point, the internal bond prevents the two proteins from forming the necessary temporary interactions that lead to a stable complex.
Furthermore, the new glutamate building block carries a negative electrical charge that clashes with the already negative surface of the TRAF6 protein.
This electrical repulsion acts like two matching ends of a magnet pushing away from each other, further blocking the proteins from coming together.
By disrupting these delicate and temporary protein-to-protein associations, the bacteria can successfully shut down the host's ability to fight off the infection.
These findings provide a detailed look at how a small chemical change after a protein is made can completely alter its shape and stability.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Working memory arises from interactions across large brain networks.
Brain wave synchronization helps coordinate long-distance communication for memory.
Used tACS to externally control brain waves in the frontoparietal network.
Artificial synchronization boosted performance during difficult tasks.
fMRI showed stimulation effects depend on timing and current mental state.
Synchronous stimulation increased parietal activity and improved behavior.
Stimulation timing changes how information flows through the memory network.
Study proves a link between brain synchronization and memory performance.

sentences.text: Complex mental abilities like working memory, which allows us to hold and use information over short periods, do not happen in just one spot in the brain.
Instead, these functions emerge from the coordinated interactions of many different brain regions working together as a large-scale network.
Scientists believe that the brain coordinates these long-distance communications by synchronizing the rhythmic electrical pulses, or brain waves, produced by neurons.
When these waves are in sync, it acts like a shared beat that allows distant parts of the brain to exchange information more effectively for memory tasks.
This method allowed the team to externally control and align the brain waves within a specific circuit on the right side of the brain known as the frontoparietal network.
To test this idea, researchers used a technique called transcranial alternating current stimulation, or tACS, to apply mild electrical currents to the scalp.
The researchers found that when they used the stimulation to force these brain regions into a synchronized rhythm, the participants performed better on memory tests.
This improvement was most noticeable when the memory tasks were particularly difficult and required a high level of mental effort.
By using fMRI scanners to look at the brain while the stimulation was happening, the team discovered that the effects of the electrical pulses were not always the same.
The impact of the stimulation depended heavily on the exact timing of the electrical waves and whether the person was actively focused on a task or at rest.
Specifically, when the stimulation was perfectly synchronized during a verbal memory task, it boosted activity in the parietal lobe, a key area for processing information.
The increase in activity in this specific brain region was directly linked to how much better the participants performed on the memory test.
By altering the 'phase' or alignment of the waves, the researchers could essentially tune the communication channels within the working memory system.
The study also showed that the timing of the stimulation changed the way information flowed between the front and the back of the brain's memory network.
In conclusion, these results provide strong evidence that there is a direct link between how well we can remember things and how well our brain regions synchronize their activity.
This suggests that large-scale brain synchronization is a fundamental requirement for handling demanding mental tasks efficiently.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: The RSG is vital for spatial and non-spatial tasks, but its neural mechanisms are unclear.
Optogenetics in mice showed parallel circuits in the RSG handle different types of information.
Spatial inputs from the thalamus and subiculum target small LR pyramidal cells.
Non-spatial inputs from the claustrum and cingulate target RS cells.
Specific wiring patterns in layer 1 allow these parallel streams to stay separate.
LR neurons can calculate head rotation speed from direction-only signals.
A unique cell type is specialized for spatial orientation in the RSG.

sentences.text: A specific part of the brain called the granular retrosplenial cortex, or RSG, is essential for helping animals navigate through space and perform other complex behaviors.
Despite its importance for memory and orientation, scientists do not yet fully understand the specific neural codes or communication patterns this region uses to process information.
They discovered that the outer layers of the RSG contain two separate, parallel circuits that handle very different types of incoming signals at the same time.
To investigate this, researchers used a technique called optogenetics in mice, which uses light to control specific brain cells and map their connections.

One circuit receives spatial information from brain areas like the anterior thalamus and the dorsal subiculum, which specifically activate a unique group of small cells known as low-rheobase pyramidal neurons.
In contrast, a different set of neighboring cells called regular-spiking neurons are controlled by inputs from the claustrum and the anterior cingulate cortex.
These specific inputs carry mostly non-spatial information, showing that the brain keeps these two streams of data separate even though the neurons live right next to each other.
This parallel processing is made possible by the highly organized way that the branches of these neurons, called axons and dendrites, are arranged within the first layer of the RSG.
By looking at how these connections function, the researchers used computer models to show that the low-rheobase neurons can actually calculate how fast an animal is turning its head.
Remarkably, these neurons can figure out the speed of rotation even though the signals they receive from the thalamus only describe the direction the head is facing, not how fast it is moving.
By identifying these distinct input streams and cell types, the study provides a clearer picture of how the brain maintains our sense of direction and processes the world around us.
These findings reveal that the RSG contains a specialized type of neuron that is perfectly positioned to transform simple compass-like signals into the complex data needed for spatial orientation.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Consistent flower shapes are vital for reproduction and resist environmental changes.
Arabidopsis thaliana always has the same number of petals.
Cardamine hirsuta has varying petal numbers, and the genetic reason is unknown.
Differences in the AP1 gene explain the difference in petal number stability between species.
Arabidopsis AP1 masks other genetic variations that would otherwise cause petal numbers to change.
The C. hirsuta version of AP1 cannot stabilize petal numbers, partly due to its control regions.
C. hirsuta keeps its variable petal count even though it has the genetic potential for four petals.

sentences.text: For many plants, having a consistent and predictable flower shape is essential for successful reproduction because it helps attract specific pollinators.
These floral forms are usually very stable and do not change even when the plant faces natural disturbances or environmental stress.
A classic example of this stability is found in the small weed Arabidopsis thaliana, which almost always produces flowers with exactly four petals.
However, in a very close relative called Cardamine hirsuta, or hairy bittercress, the number of petals can vary significantly from one flower to the next.
Until recently, scientists did not understand the specific genetic reasons why these two related species have such different levels of petal consistency.
Researchers have now discovered that changes in a single master-regulator gene called APETALA1, or AP1 for short, are responsible for this difference.
By masking these other genes, the Arabidopsis AP1 ensures that every flower develops the same number of petals regardless of other internal genetic noise.
The study shows that the version of the AP1 gene found in Arabidopsis acts like a shield that hides the effects of other minor genetic variations.
In contrast, the version of the AP1 gene in hairy bittercress lacks this stabilizing ability and cannot perform the same protective function.
This failure to stabilize the trait is partly due to differences in the regulatory regions of the DNA that control when and where the AP1 gene is turned on.

Interestingly, hairy bittercress continues to produce flowers with varying petal numbers even though it possesses enough natural genetic diversity to potentially produce flowers with a stable count of four petals.
This suggests that the plant maintains its variable petal count as a distinct trait, even when the genetic building blocks for a more consistent form are present in the population.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Digestive system function and repair are essential for most animals.
Used LCM and RNA-seq to study the gut of the planarian Schmidtea mediterranea, which can regenerate its entire body.
Found hundreds of new genes active in the intestine that were previously missed.
Digestive biology and cell types are highly similar between planarians and other animals like humans.
Discovered regional gene expression patterns across the gut, particularly in goblet cells.
Identified gli-1 and RREB2 as factors controlling goblet cell regeneration and maintenance.
The study provides a foundation for future research into gut health and repair.

sentences.text: For almost every animal on Earth, the ability to maintain a healthy digestive system and repair it after damage is essential for survival.
In this study, researchers focused on a flatworm called Schmidtea mediterranea, a remarkable creature known for its ability to regrow any part of its body, including its entire gut.
To understand how this works, the team used a precise technique called laser-capture microdissection to isolate specific gut tissues and then analyzed the genetic activity within those samples.
By using these advanced tools, the scientists were able to identify hundreds of genes active in the worm's intestine that had never been detected by earlier research methods.

When they compared these findings to other species, they discovered that the basic biology of digestion and the types of cells involved are very similar across the animal kingdom, including in humans.
The study also revealed that the planarian gut is much more organized than previously thought, with different genes being active in different areas of the intestine.
This regional organization was especially clear in a group of cells known as goblet cells, which showed distinct genetic patterns depending on their location.
Furthermore, the researchers pinpointed two specific proteins that act as master switches for these goblet cells.
One of these proteins, called gli-1, is necessary for the worm to regrow new goblet cells during regeneration, while another called RREB2 is required to keep existing cells healthy and functional.
By creating this detailed map of the gut, the research provides a valuable new resource for scientists studying how the digestive tract functions and heals.
Ultimately, these insights into the flatworm's incredible healing powers could help us better understand how to treat gastrointestinal diseases and improve tissue repair in humans.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Mitochondria need quality control to remove misfolded proteins for health.
Mitochondrial quality control pathways are not well understood.
Used temperature-sensitive proteins in yeast as a model for study.
Specific proteins are broken down by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
Ubr1 and San1 are the specific enzymes that tag these proteins.
Chaperones like Hsp70 and Sis1 are required for this degradation.
Cdc48 complex, Doa1, and Ubx2 are also involved in the process.
This pathway is unique because it mixes cytosolic and mitochondrial factors.

sentences.text: If these misfolded proteins are allowed to build up, they can become toxic and prevent the mitochondria from producing the energy the cell needs to survive.
Mitochondria are the powerhouses of the cell, and for them to function correctly, the cell must have a way to find and get rid of proteins that have folded into the wrong shapes.
Despite how important this process is, scientists have not yet fully understood the specific pathways the cell uses to manage quality control for proteins located on the surface of the mitochondria.
They specifically engineered these proteins to be temperature-sensitive, meaning the proteins would only begin to misfold and trigger the cell's cleanup response when the temperature was raised.
To investigate this, researchers used baker's yeast as a model organism and focused on specific proteins found on the outer membrane of the mitochondria.

The study found that two specific proteins, named sen2-1HAts and sam35-2HAts, are removed from the mitochondrial surface and broken down by a cellular disposal system known as the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
In this disposal process, the cell uses special enzymes called ubiquitin ligases to attach a molecular 'trash tag' to the faulty proteins so they can be recognized for destruction.
The researchers discovered that a ligase called Ubr1 is responsible for tagging the sen2-1HAts protein, while a different ligase called San1 is the primary one that tags the sam35-2HAts protein.
Furthermore, the study showed that this mitochondrial degradation process requires the help of molecular 'chaperones,' specifically those from the SSA family and another called Sis1.
This discovery is significant because it provides the very first evidence that these chaperone proteins are actively involved in the quality control of proteins at the mitochondria.

The researchers also identified several other components necessary for the cleanup, including a protein complex called Cdc48-Npl4-Ufd1, a protein named Doa1, and a specific pool of the protein Ubx2 that is located right on the mitochondrial membrane.
By putting all these pieces together, the study reveals a unique quality control pathway that uses a specific mix of factors from both the main body of the cell and the mitochondria themselves.
This particular combination of machinery makes this mitochondrial pathway distinct from the quality control systems used in other parts of the cell, such as the nucleus or the endoplasmic reticulum.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: MicroRNAs regulate gene expression and miR-9 is highly abundant in the brain.
miR-9's role in early neural cells is known, but its role in dendrites and synapses is not.
Developed a 'sponge' mouse model to turn off miR-9 in specific places and times.
Found that miR-9 controls how dendrites grow and how signals are sent across synapses.
miR-9 works by reducing the protein REST, which is necessary for dendrite growth.

sentences.text: MicroRNAs are small molecules that help control how genes are turned on or off within a cell after the initial genetic instructions are read.
One specific type, known as miR-9, is found in very high amounts throughout the brain compared to other parts of the body.
Scientists already understand how miR-9 helps early-stage brain stem cells develop, but they did not know how it affects the later growth of a neuron's branches and connections.
Specifically, the role of this molecule in the formation of dendrites, which receive signals, and synapses, which transmit them, remained a mystery.
This tool allowed the team to soak up and deactivate the miR-9 family in specific parts of the brain at exact times during the mouse's development.
To study this in living animals, the researchers created a special type of genetically modified mouse called a 'sponge' line.
By using this new method, the researchers discovered that miR-9 is essential for controlling how the tree-like branches of neurons grow.
They also found that this microRNA is necessary for the proper transmission of electrical signals between these brain cells.
Reducing the amount of this REST protein is a vital step that allows the neuron's branches to grow and develop correctly.
The study further revealed that miR-9 works by lowering the levels of a protein called REST, which normally acts as a brake on gene activity.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Diseases spread by insects peak at middle temperatures and drop at extremes.
Created a model for Ross River virus, a mosquito-borne threat in Australia and the Pacific.
Transmission is highest at 26.4°C.
Transmission stops at the lower limit of 17.0°C.
Transmission stops at the upper limit of 31.5°C.
Model predicts year-round spread in tropics and seasonal spread in temperate zones.
Warming will increase spread in temperate areas but decrease it in the tropics.
Nonlinear models are vital for understanding climate change impacts on disease.

sentences.text: According to the principles of thermal biology, diseases carried by insects or other vectors do not spread at a constant rate across all environments.
Instead, the transmission of these diseases usually reaches a peak at moderate, intermediate temperatures and falls off significantly when conditions become either too hot or too cold.
This specific pathogen is a major mosquito-borne threat throughout Australia and the Pacific Islands, and health experts are concerned it could eventually emerge in other parts of the world.
To better understand these patterns, researchers developed a new mathematical model to track the thermal responses of the Ross River virus.
The study found that the transmission of the virus is most efficient when the temperature is around 26.4°C.
As temperatures move away from this ideal middle point, the ability of the virus to spread begins to decline.
The model shows that transmission effectively stops once the environment cools down to a lower limit of 17.0°C.
On the other end of the spectrum, the spread of the disease also drops to zero when temperatures rise above a maximum limit of 31.5°C.
These regional differences explain why there is a distinct seasonal spike in human infections across the entire country at certain times of the year.

As the planet warms due to climate change, the model suggests that transmission will likely increase in temperate zones where the majority of Australians live.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Beta oscillations in the motor cortex have been known for a long time, but their exact role in behavior is still not understood.

sentences.text: Even though these brain waves are a well-known phenomenon, researchers have struggled to determine exactly how they relate to the way we move our bodies or what specific behaviors they control.
For many decades, scientists have observed specific rhythmic patterns of electrical activity in the brain's motor cortex known as beta oscillations.
The researchers recorded neural activity across multiple scales while the monkeys participated in a specialized neurofeedback task designed to give them control over their own brain signals.
To solve this mystery and understand the connection between large groups of neurons, beta waves, and physical actions, a team of researchers conducted a study using three macaque monkeys.
During these experiments, the monkeys were trained to use their willpower to adjust the strength of their beta oscillations to a specific level requested by the researchers.
Once the monkeys successfully reached the target brain state, they were then required to perform a physical task by reaching out with their arms.
In contrast, when the monkeys increased their beta wave power, there was a noticeable delay, and it took them much longer to begin the reaching motion.
The results showed a clear difference in timing: when the monkeys reduced their beta wave power, they were able to start their arm movements significantly faster.
The researchers discovered that when beta oscillations were high—whether the monkeys created them on purpose or they happened naturally—the collective activity of the neurons shifted.
This shift moved the brain's overall state further away from the specific configuration of neural activity that is required to actually trigger a movement.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Sulforaphane (SFN) from vegetables activates Nrf2 to change gene expression.
SFN blocks HIV in macrophages but not in T cells.
SFN blocks HIV in specific cell lines; removing Nrf2 increases infection and stops SFN's effect.
Anti-viral activity is driven by Nrf2 after SFN activates it.
SFN stops HIV after entry but before genetic material forms circles.
Known anti-viral proteins SAMHD1 and MX2 were not increased.
Nrf2 can strongly block HIV, offering a new way to stop the virus.

sentences.text: Sulforaphane is a natural compound found in cruciferous vegetables like broccoli and cabbage that is released when the plants are chopped or chewed.
This compound works by activating a protein called Nrf2, which moves into the cell nucleus to significantly change how genes are expressed.
However, this protective effect was not seen in primary T cells, another type of immune cell that HIV commonly targets.
In this study, researchers discovered for the first time that sulforaphane can successfully stop HIV from infecting primary macrophages, which are key immune cells.
Furthermore, removing Nrf2 prevented sulforaphane from working, which confirms that the anti-viral benefits of the vegetable compound depend entirely on this specific protein.
The researchers also observed that sulforaphane blocked the virus in specific lab-grown immune cell lines, but it did not have this effect in other types of cells they tested.
When the team used genetic tools to remove Nrf2 from the macrophages, the virus was able to infect the cells much more easily.
These findings support a biological model where the body's own anti-viral defenses are triggered by Nrf2 once it has been mobilized by sulforaphane.

The study further pinpointed exactly when the virus is stopped; sulforaphane treatment allows the virus to enter the cell but blocks it before it can form the circular DNA structures needed for a permanent infection.
This timing is similar to how other known anti-viral proteins like SAMHD1 and MX2 work to protect our cells from infection.
Interestingly, the researchers found that sulforaphane did not actually increase the levels of those specific well-known anti-viral proteins.
This suggests that Nrf2 is using a different, previously unknown pathway to fight off the virus.
Overall, this research demonstrates for the first time that activating Nrf2 can powerfully inhibit HIV infection.
These results highlight a promising new strategy for triggering the body's natural defenses to stop the virus from spreading.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Viruses spread by Aedes mosquitoes cause outbreaks globally.
Zika following dengue in the Dominican Republic allowed for a comparison of how these viruses spread.
Dengue mostly affected young people under 20, while Zika was found across all age groups.
Zika cases were significantly more common in women than in men.
The rate of Zika infection in women was nearly three times higher than the rate in men.
Guillain-Barré syndrome, a serious condition linked to Zika, was slightly more common in men.
Having had dengue before did not seem to protect the population from getting Zika.
The high number of cases in women is likely due to health campaigns encouraging them to see doctors, though biological factors are possible.
Public health efforts should focus on testing and informing women of childbearing age during outbreaks.

sentences.text: Viruses that are carried and spread by Aedes mosquitoes continue to cause major disease outbreaks in many parts of the world.

In the Dominican Republic, a large outbreak of the Zika virus occurred immediately after a major dengue epidemic, which gave researchers a unique chance to compare how these two similar viruses spread through the same population.
The study found that while 75% of reported dengue cases occurred in young people under the age of 20, Zika infections were much more evenly spread across people of all different ages.
A very high proportion of the reported Zika infections—nearly 74%—were found among women.
When looking at the infection rates adjusted for age, women had a rate of 7.64 cases per 10,000 people, which was significantly higher than the rate of 2.72 cases per 10,000 people seen in men.
Interestingly, the rate of Guillain-Barré syndrome, a rare neurological condition often triggered by Zika, was actually slightly higher in men than in women.
The data also suggested that having immunity from a previous dengue infection did not have a significant impact on whether or not people caught the Zika virus at a population level.

The researchers believe the most likely reason for the high number of reported cases in women is that public health awareness campaigns encouraged women of reproductive age to seek medical care more often, though they cannot completely rule out that women might be biologically more susceptible to the virus.
Because of these findings, it is recommended that health officials use media campaigns and increased medical screening specifically for women of reproductive age during future Zika outbreaks.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Anabaena filaments develop a pattern of heterocysts when nitrogen is scarce.
Study of HetR expression fluctuations using a fluorescent marker in both nitrogen-rich and nitrogen-poor conditions.
HetR fluctuations are coupled between nearby cells within a range of two to three cells.
Cell-to-cell correlations come from molecular transfer rather than cell division.
Fluctuations under nitrogen-poor conditions build upon existing fluctuations from nitrogen-rich conditions.
PatS, SepJ, and HetR auto-regulation determine fluctuations in nitrogen-rich conditions.

sentences.text: This process results in specialized nitrogen-fixing cells, called heterocysts, appearing at regular intervals of about ten normal cells along the filament.
When the cyanobacterium Anabaena lacks nitrogen, its long chains of cells undergo a developmental change to create a specific pattern.
To understand how this happens, we tracked the activity of a key protein called HetR by attaching a fluorescent marker to it, allowing us to see how its levels fluctuated in individual cells.
We measured these fluctuations both when nitrogen was plentiful and at various times after nitrogen was removed from the environment.
Our analysis showed that the variations in HetR levels in one cell are linked to the levels in its neighbors, typically affecting a range of two to three nearby cells.
These connections between cells are mainly caused by molecules moving directly from cell to cell rather than being passed down when a cell divides.
We also discovered that the patterns of gene activity that emerge when nitrogen is scarce actually build upon the random fluctuations already present when nitrogen is abundant.

In environments with plenty of nitrogen, the way HetR levels vary is controlled by a specific inhibitor called PatS, a communication protein called SepJ, and the ability of HetR to increase its own production.
By comparing different conditions, we identified distinct roles for the inhibitors PatS and HetN, as well as differences in how communication proteins like SepJ and FraC/FraD function.

Ultimately, our findings show how these different proteins work together alongside the natural randomness of gene activity to coordinate the cell-to-cell interactions that form the final developmental pattern.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Humans can learn multiple motor mappings when feedback alternates.
Context cues help switch between these mappings.
Little is known about how these associations are learned and generalized.
Participants did a pointing task with manipulated visual feedback.
Feedback offsets depended on the target's shape.
Shapes were morphed between spiky and circular.
Testing occurred on new shapes without feedback.
Two hypotheses were compared.
Hypothesis 1: Explicit extraction of a linear relationship.
Hypothesis 2: Implicit Bayesian model based on categorization.
Results support the Bayesian model; people use the most similar trained mapping.
Learning slows down with more training pairs, as predicted.
The Bayesian model is a likely mechanism for learning multiple mappings.

sentences.text: People have the ability to learn and store several different ways of moving to reach a goal, a process known as dual-adaptation, when they receive alternating feedback for each movement.
By learning specific cues from the environment, humans can quickly switch between these different stored movement patterns to suit the current situation.
However, scientists do not yet fully understand how we learn the link between a cue and a specific movement, or how we apply that learning to new but similar situations.
To explore this, researchers asked participants to perform a fast-paced pointing task where the visual feedback of their hand position was intentionally shifted away from where they actually moved.
The amount of this horizontal shift changed depending on the shape of the target the person was trying to hit.
The targets used in the study were chosen from a range of shapes that gradually changed, or morphed, from very spiky to very circular.
After the initial training phase, the researchers tested how well participants could hit new shapes they had never seen before without providing any visual feedback on their performance.
The study compared two different ideas about how people might handle these new shapes.
The first hypothesis was that people would consciously figure out the mathematical relationship between a shape and the required movement to hit it.

The second hypothesis used a computer model called a Bayesian learning model, which suggested that people would instead categorize the new shape and simply use the movement associated with the most similar shape they already knew.

The results showed that while people need to be aware of the cues to learn them, they ultimately choose their movements based on which trained shape is most similar to the current one, which supports the Bayesian model.
Additionally, the Bayesian model predicted that learning would become slower as the number of different shape-movement pairs increased, a trend that was clearly seen in the experimental data.

In conclusion, the strong match between the computer model and the actual behavior of participants suggests that this model explains how the brain manages to learn multiple movement patterns at the same time.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Many countries cannot start or expand NTD programs because they lack basic data for planning.
We created and tested a new combined mapping method (ITM) for four specific tropical diseases.
The method saves resources and identifies if infection levels are high enough to require treatment.
The protocol uses standard WHO health markers for specific age groups.
We compared our new method against standard WHO methods in Mali and Senegal.
We looked at treatment decisions, ease of use, and total costs.
The new method gave the same results for three diseases but was more precise for schistosomiasis.
The integrated method was practical and cheaper than using separate standard methods.
This tool can help countries launch important health programs more easily.

sentences.text: Despite the availability of treatments, many countries where neglected tropical diseases are common have struggled to start or expand health programs because they do not have the basic data needed for planning and advocacy.

To address this, we developed and tested a new combined mapping approach called the Integrated Threshold Mapping (ITM) methodology to track four different conditions: lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and intestinal worms.
This new protocol was specifically designed to use resources efficiently while determining if the level of infection in a community has reached the point where public health treatments must begin.
The system relies on health indicators already recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) and focuses on the specific age groups most affected by each disease.
We put this protocol to the test by comparing its performance against the current standard WHO mapping methods in one district in Mali and one district in Senegal.
During the trial, we compared the two different approaches based on the treatment decisions they led to, how easy they were to carry out, and the total financial costs involved.

The results showed that our integrated methodology reached the exact same conclusions as the standard methods for trachoma, lymphatic filariasis, and intestinal worms, while providing even more specific and targeted treatment recommendations for schistosomiasis.

Our findings demonstrate that the integrated mapping tool is practical and feasible to use, and it saved a significant amount of money compared to using the standard, separate mapping methods for each disease.
Ultimately, this combined mapping tool could make it much easier for countries where these diseases are widespread to launch the essential health programs their citizens need.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: Aging reduces stem cell numbers in their niche, but the reasons why are not well known.
Notch signaling increases with age in fruit fly germline stem cells, causing them to leave the niche.
Low Notch levels increase cell stickiness via E-cadherin, helping cells stay in the niche better than neighbors.
Artificially raising Notch speeds up stem cell loss, a process partly controlled by the Sex lethal protein.
Notch activity decreases in the niche itself with age, showing it controls cell retention from both inside and outside the stem cells.
These findings show how Notch regulates aging-related cell adhesion and may explain how cancer cells spread.

sentences.text: As organs grow older, the number of stem cells living in their specialized protective environments, known as niches, tends to decrease.
Scientists have long observed this decline, but the specific biological mechanisms that cause stem cells to leave these niches during aging are not yet fully understood.
In this study, researchers found that a specific communication pathway called Notch signaling becomes more active as female fruit flies age.
This increase in Notch signaling in the germline stem cells directly leads to their removal from the niche over time.
By comparing different cells, the team discovered that stem cells with lower Notch levels are stickier and can out-compete their neighbors to stay in the niche.
This stickiness is controlled by a protein called E-cadherin, which acts like a glue to hold the cells in place.
They also found that this loss is partially driven by another protein known as Sex lethal, which helps manage the cell's response to aging.
When the researchers artificially boosted Notch signaling, the stem cells were lost from the niche much faster than normal.
Because Notch signaling in the niche is required to keep the environment stable, this decrease further contributes to the loss of stem cells from both the inside and the outside.
Interestingly, while Notch signaling goes up in the stem cells, it actually goes down in the surrounding niche cells as the fly ages.
These results reveal a new way that Notch signaling controls how well stem cells can hold onto their homes during the aging process.
This discovery is also important for cancer research, as similar Notch signaling changes can help metastatic cancer cells break away and spread to other parts of the body.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: HIV is currently incurable but manageable with drug combinations.
Different viral genetics in patients make choosing the right drug mix difficult.
Genetic and clinical data allow for computer models to predict best treatments.
Current models only use viral genetics and ignore drug chemistry.
We used proteochemometric models to combine drug and protein properties.
The study used a massive dataset of 300,000 data points and thousands of mutants.
The models achieved a very low prediction error.
The new models outperformed older sequence-only models in predicting resistance.

Proteochemometric models accurately predict resistance even for new viral types.

sentences.text: While there is currently no cure for HIV infection, the virus can be managed effectively using a combination of several different anti-viral medications.

Because the genetic makeup of the virus is slightly different in almost every patient, doctors face the difficult challenge of deciding which specific combination of drugs will work best for each individual.

By using large amounts of genetic data from the virus and clinical information from patients, researchers can now build computer programs that help predict the most effective treatment plan for a person.
Most existing computer models only look at the genetic sequence of the virus, but they fail to consider the chemical characteristics of the drugs themselves.
To see if including drug chemistry would help, we used a method called proteochemometric modeling, which looks at both the properties of the drugs and the viral proteins they target at the same time.
We tested this approach using a massive clinical database containing 300,000 data points that tracked how different drugs interacted with tens of thousands of unique viral mutants.
Our results showed that these new models were highly accurate, with a very low margin of error when predicting how well a drug would work.
When we compared our new method to older models that only used genetic sequences, our approach was significantly better at identifying which viruses would be resistant to treatment.
Additionally, we were able to confirm known genetic changes that cause drug resistance and even discovered several new mutations in the virus that had never been reported before.
We also tested our model on a public database from Stanford University and achieved a correct prediction rate of 84%, which is higher than the 80% achieved by previous high-quality studies.
We conclude that this modeling approach is a powerful tool for accurately predicting drug resistance, even when dealing with new or complex mixtures of viral mutations.
Finally, we have added a feature to the system that tells the user exactly how much they can trust each specific prediction, providing a measure of reliability for clinical use.

sentences.text: The dengue virus is currently the most common virus spread by insects, resulting in approximately 100 million people developing symptoms every year.
Infection with this virus can lead to a wide range of health issues, from a relatively mild condition known as dengue fever to a much more dangerous form called dengue hemorrhagic fever.

The most severe symptoms usually appear during a critical window about five to seven days after the fever starts, but scientists do not yet fully understand what causes some patients to progress from the mild form to the life-threatening version.

To investigate this, researchers used a specialized technique called mass spectrometry to analyze the blood chemistry of adult patients during both the most dangerous phase of the illness and the recovery period.

The study identified 29 specific small molecules, or metabolites, that were present at different levels in patients with severe dengue compared to those with the milder form during the critical phase.
These molecules included various substances such as bile acids, purines, fats called phospholipids, and amino acids.
Bile acids were found to be up to five times higher in patients with severe dengue, and these high levels were linked to specific enzymes that indicate the liver has been injured.
The researchers also looked at uric acid, which is the most common natural antioxidant found in human blood.
They discovered that uric acid levels were 1.5 times lower in the severe cases than in the mild cases.
This drop in uric acid likely weakens the body's natural defenses against damage, leading to increased internal stress at the cellular level.

Even when patients were in the recovery phase, eight of these molecules remained at abnormal levels in the severe group, including a specific bile acid that suggests the liver may suffer long-lasting effects from the infection.
Overall, the study highlights how the body's internal chemical processes change during severe dengue and provides new information on how the virus interacts with the human host.
These findings improve our knowledge of how severe dengue develops and point toward new possibilities for creating treatments to better manage the disease.

abstract_claim_plan.core_claim: The amount of substrate receptors in CRLs must be strictly regulated to keep the full variety of CRLs available.
If levels are unbalanced, a few too-common receptors can hog the core components of the CRL.
Many diseases like cancer are linked to problems with these receptor levels, especially in SCF ligases.
One way F-box protein levels are controlled is through self-destruction by the full SCF complex.
A new pathway breaks down the Met30 protein when it is not attached to Skp1.
This pathway uses the Cdc53/Cul1 component but surprisingly does not need Skp1.
This unusual breakdown process is vital for keeping chromosomes stable and protecting against toxic heavy metals.
The results show that a specific sub-group of proteins (Cdc53/Rbx1/Cdc34) has its own important biological job without Skp1.

sentences.text: Cells must carefully control the amount of specific receptor proteins used by Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases (CRLs) to ensure that the full variety of these molecular machines remains available for different tasks.
If these levels become unbalanced, a few overabundant receptors can essentially hijack the core parts of the ligase, preventing other necessary receptors from working.

When these receptor components are not regulated correctly, it can lead to many different diseases, including various types of cancer, particularly within the largest group of these ligases known as SCF ligases.
One known way the cell manages the levels of these receptors, called F-box proteins, is by having the complete SCF complex trigger their own destruction through a process called ubiquitylation.
In this study using yeast, researchers discovered a different pathway that breaks down an F-box protein called Met30 specifically when it is separated from its usual partner protein, Skp1.
Surprisingly, this specific degradation process requires a core component called Cdc53/Cul1 but functions entirely without the help of the other major component, Skp1.
The researchers proved that this unusual breakdown pathway is essential for maintaining the stability of chromosomes and for helping the cell defend itself against the stress caused by heavy metals.
Most importantly, these findings reveal that a smaller sub-complex consisting of Cdc53, Rbx1, and Cdc34 has its own critical biological functions that do not depend on the presence of Skp1.
